name: Face slimming supplements / teas
summary: Herbal teas and capsules sold for a slimmer face; no trial has tested them for facial fat and some herbal slimming ingredients have been banned.
lead: Face slimming supplements and teas are herbal products marketed or discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness or fat, usually through claims of diuretic, laxative, metabolism-boosting or detox effects. They are sold under the broader heading of herbal and dietary weight-loss products.

name: Ketogenic diet face
summary: Keto for a leaner face: a real diet with epilepsy origins; weight-loss advantage is small and no study covers the face.
lead: The ketogenic diet face refers to the belief in appearance communities that a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat ketogenic diet leans out the face, reducing puffiness and cheek fat. The diet itself restricts carbohydrate so that the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel, and was developed in the 1920s as a treatment for epilepsy.

name: OMAD / 36-hour fasts
summary: One meal a day or 36-hour fasts for fast fat loss; intermittent fasting has modest evidence and health bodies call it inconclusive.
lead: OMAD (one meal a day) is a form of time-restricted eating in which all daily food is eaten in a window of one to two hours; 36-hour fasts extend the pause between meals beyond a day. Both are used in looksmaxxing communities to lose body fat quickly and get a leaner face.
claims: OMAD with low carbohydrate is a fast way to get lean
OMAD at about 1,500 calories does not cause hair loss

name: Cardio / zone 2 for leanness
summary: Steady aerobic exercise for fat loss; well-established for health, with zone 2 specifically still debated for leanness.
lead: Cardio for leanness is the use of aerobic exercise, including low-intensity steady-state work often called zone 2, to lose body fat and look leaner. Zone 2 has no universally accepted definition but is commonly placed at roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate, where fat is the main fuel and lactate is cleared about as fast as it is produced.

name: Water fasting
summary: Multi-day zero-calorie fasting for fast fat loss; documented risks include refeeding syndrome and loss of lean tissue.
lead: Water fasting, also called extended or zero-calorie fasting, is abstaining from all food and caloric drinks for 24 hours or more, usually several days. In looksmaxxing communities it is used for rapid fat loss and with claims about skin and facial leanness.
claims: Water fasting strips fat faster than eating less

name: T3 / thyroid fat loss
summary: Using the thyroid hormone liothyronine (T3) off-label to cut body fat; the drug label says it is ineffective for weight loss at normal doses and risky at high ones.
lead: Liothyronine is a synthetic form of triiodothyronine (T3), the more active of the two main thyroid hormones. It was approved for medical use in 1956 and is used mainly for hypothyroidism and myxedema coma.

name: Ephedrine / ECA stack
summary: A stimulant combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used for cutting; trials show modest short-term fat loss with cardiovascular risk.
lead: The ECA stack combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is described as popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions. A looksmax.org guide describes it as a stack for metabolism increase, appetite suppression and energy, to assist weight loss.
claims: ECA raises metabolism and suppresses appetite for fat loss.
ECA should be combined with exercise to be worthwhile.

name: DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol)
summary: An industrial mitochondrial uncoupler that burns fat as heat, banned for human use since 1938 and tied to documented deaths.
lead: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is an industrial chemical that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, converting food energy into heat rather than stored chemical energy. It was marketed as a weight-loss drug in the United States in the 1930s and was judged too toxic for human consumption under the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
claims: DNP produces very fast fat loss over a few weeks.
The dangers are manageable with hydration and avoiding hot weather.
DNP stacked with GLP-1 drugs, testosterone or other agents is an efficient cutting combination.

name: Fat grafting for facial asymmetry
summary: Moving a patient's own fat into the leaner side of the face to even out volume; common in surgery, but graft survival is unpredictable.
lead: Fat grafting, or fat transfer, moves a person's own fat from one area to another. It has three stages: harvesting, usually by liposuction, processing, and reinjection. It is used in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery for volume replacement, including the face.

name: Ptosis surgery for asymmetry
summary: Eyelid-lifting surgery to correct a drooping upper lid so the eyes match; an established procedure, with uneven lids a recognised complication.
lead: Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid, caused by dysfunction of the levator muscle, its nerve supply, or the sympathetic supply to Muller's muscle. Causes include aging, congenital factors, trauma and underlying conditions such as myasthenia gravis. Ptosis surgery for asymmetry refers to repairing a lower-set lid so that the two eyes look more alike.

name: Bilateral chewing habit
summary: Deliberately alternating the chewing side in the hope of keeping the jaw and face symmetrical; no studies found on the claim.
lead: The bilateral chewing habit is the practice of alternating the side used for chewing. Chewing is mostly unconscious, but conscious input can influence it, and feedback from nerves in the teeth and jaw joints helps control how long and how forcefully each muscle acts.

name: Unilateral chewing correction
summary: Deliberately chewing on both sides to fix a one-sided habit people blame for facial asymmetry; the cause-and-effect link is untested.
lead: Unilateral chewing correction is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person who habitually chews on one side of the mouth tries to chew on both sides, or to use the less-used side more, in the hope of reducing facial asymmetry. It is a behavioural habit change and involves no product or procedure.

name: Flipped mirror selfie check
summary: Comparing a flipped and unflipped photo of your face to see how others see you; the idea rests on familiarity effects, and the practice itself is unstudied.
lead: A flipped mirror selfie check is a looksmaxxing habit of comparing a person's mirror-reversed face with a true (non-reversed) photo. People do this because the face seen in a mirror every day differs in left-right orientation from the face others see in person or in photographs.

name: Symmetry photo mirroring tools
summary: Apps and editors that build left-left and right-right face composites to visualise asymmetry; a research method with known artefacts.
lead: Symmetry photo mirroring tools produce composite images from a single face photograph by mirroring its left half or right half across the midline, yielding a left-left and a right-right version. Looksmaxxing communities use them to visualise asymmetry and to compare the composites with the unaltered face.

name: Back sleeping pillow setup
summary: Using pillows to stay on your back at night, which looksmaxxers hope will even out one-sided facial changes; no study tests that outcome.
lead: A back sleeping pillow setup is an arrangement of pillows meant to keep a sleeper lying on the back instead of on one side or the stomach. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to avoid pressure on one side of the face overnight.
claims: Sleeping on one side causes the "bad" side of the face to look worse

name: Chiropractic neck adjustment
summary: High-velocity neck manipulation sometimes sought for posture and jaw or face alignment; case reports link it to arterial injury and stroke.
lead: A chiropractic neck adjustment, or cervical spinal manipulation, is a thrust technique applied to the joints of the neck. It is used for neck pain and is also discussed in appearance-related communities in connection with posture and head alignment.

name: Craniosacral therapy
summary: Light-touch skull and spine manipulation based on a claimed cranial rhythm; reviews find the evidence weak and the premise at odds with anatomy.
lead: Craniosacral therapy (CST) is a form of alternative medicine in which practitioners use light touch to feel purported rhythmic movements of the skull bones and spine and to adjust them. It grew out of cranial osteopathy devised by William Garner Sutherland in the early twentieth century, and was developed by osteopath John Upledger, who ran research on the purported pulse at Michigan State University between 1975 and 1983 .
claims: The skull flexes and extends in a craniosacral rhythm driven by the sphenoid and occipital bones

name: Myofascial release / Rolfing
summary: Hands-on fascia manipulation, best known as Rolfing, said by practitioners to realign posture and the body (and, in some circles, the face); trial evidence is thin and of low certainty.
lead: Rolfing, formally known as Structural Integration, is a system of manual therapy developed by the biochemist Ida P. Rolf (1896-1979) beginning in the 1940s. It is typically delivered as a ten-session series in which a practitioner applies slow, deep pressure to connective tissue (fascia) while guiding the client's movement, with the stated aim of improving alignment relative to gravity.

name: TMJ splint (orthotic)
summary: A custom dental splint worn to stabilize or reposition the jaw joint; used for TMJ disorders, with modest and debated evidence and no research on appearance outcomes.
lead: A TMJ splint, also called an occlusal splint, bite splint or night guard, is a removable dental appliance molded to the upper or lower teeth. It is used to protect teeth, manage temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders, stabilize the joint, or alter the bite position.

name: TMJ Botox
summary: Botulinum toxin injected into jaw muscles to ease temporomandibular disorders and bruxism; trials exist but results are mixed in the sources and it is off-label in most places.
lead: TMJ Botox is the use of botulinum toxin injections in the jaw muscles to treat temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD), bruxism (clenching and grinding), and related jaw pain. It is performed by clinicians and is a prescription treatment.

name: Functional appliance orthodontics
summary: Braces-adjacent appliances (Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel) used in growing children to shift the lower jaw forward in Class II cases; trials show changes, with debate over how much is skeletal.
lead: Functional appliance orthodontics is a group of treatments, using devices such as the Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel (FR-2), Bionator, Bass and activator appliances, that aim to modify jaw growth and bite relationships in growing patients, most often to correct a Class II malocclusion where the lower jaw sits behind the upper.

name: Torticollis stretching
summary: Stretching and physical therapy for a tight sternocleidomastoid; established for infant congenital torticollis, while its use for adult head tilt or facial symmetry is not studied in the sources.
lead: Torticollis, commonly called wry neck, is a condition in which neck muscles, most often the sternocleidomastoid, produce an abnormal tilt, turn or flexion of the head. It may be congenital, acquired, or spasmodic (cervical dystonia).

name: Cranial remolding helmet
summary: A custom infant helmet used for skull flattening (plagiocephaly); studies exist but high-quality evidence on benefit beyond natural improvement is described as lacking.
lead: A cranial remolding helmet, also called a cranial orthosis, is a custom helmet worn by infants to treat positional (deformational) plagiocephaly, in which the skull is flattened on one side or at the back. It is typically used between about 3 and 18 months of age after conservative care such as repositioning has not corrected the shape.

name: Scoliosis / pelvic tilt correction
summary: Efforts to manage spinal curvature and pelvic alignment that some forum users link to shoulder, eye-line and height asymmetry; clinical care exists, but cosmetic payoffs are barely studied.
lead: Scoliosis is a three-dimensional curvature of the spine, usually defined as a Cobb angle above 10 degrees on a radiograph . Pelvic tilt is the forward or backward angulation of the pelvis, and in the spinal deformity literature it is treated as one of the key radiographic parameters alongside truncal inclination and sagittal balance . In looksmaxxing communities the two are discussed together as the postural base on which shoulders, neck, head position and apparent facial balance sit.
claims: A mild scoliosis causes visible asymmetry in the eyes and trapezius.
Scoliosis surgery can add two to three inches of height and straighten the back.
Posture and pelvic alignment form a base for facial balance.

name: Alexander technique
summary: A century-old posture and movement re-education method with trial support for back and neck pain, but no studies on looks.
lead: The Alexander technique is a method of movement and posture re-education named after Frederick Matthias Alexander (1869-1955), an actor who began developing it in the 1890s to deal with voice loss during performance . It is taught in individual lessons, usually 30 to 60 minutes, using verbal cues and gentle touch during activities such as sitting, standing and walking .

name: Forward head posture exercises
summary: Neck-strengthening and chin-tuck style routines for forward head posture; studied for neck pain, with community debate over whether they help or hurt the profile.
lead: Forward head posture (FHP) is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, often accompanied by rounded shoulders and increased upper-back curvature. It is commonly called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, and is measured clinically with the craniovertebral angle . Exercises for it typically aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors and to stretch tight neck and chest muscles .
claims: Forward head posture causes problems throughout the body.
Fixing forward head posture makes a recessed chin look worse.
Forward head posture may affect maxillary growth.
Models and actors have forward head posture, so correcting it may be unnecessary.

name: Phone neck habit change
summary: Changing how you hold and look at your phone to reduce 'text neck'; research links the posture to neck pain, but nothing tests facial or neck asymmetry.
lead: Text neck is a popular name for the flexed head-and-neck posture used with phones and computers, and a cluster of symptoms attributed to it, mostly neck pain . Phone neck habit change describes changing how and how long people use devices to lessen that posture. In looksmaxxing discussion the aim is often stated as reducing neck or upper-body asymmetry.

name: Beard shaping to hide asymmetry
summary: Using beard length and outline to camouflage uneven jaw or face; a styling idea with no studies behind it.
lead: Beard shaping to hide asymmetry is the practice of trimming or outlining facial hair so that differences between the two sides of the lower face, such as an uneven jaw or chin, are less noticeable. It belongs to style-based approaches in looksmaxxing alongside haircuts and glasses.

name: Asymmetric hair part
summary: Parting hair off-centre to rebalance a face with uneven sides; a styling idea with no studies behind it.
lead: An asymmetric hair part, in looksmaxxing usage, is an off-centre parting chosen so that hair falls in a way that visually balances differences between the two sides of the face.

name: Brow microblading for symmetry
summary: A hand-applied semi-permanent brow tattoo used to even out uneven eyebrows; it fades and needs touch-ups, and no trials test it for symmetry.
lead: Brow microblading for symmetry is the use of microblading, a semi-permanent eyebrow tattoo technique, to even out differences in shape, height or fullness between a person's two eyebrows. A handheld tool with tiny needles deposits pigment into the upper dermis in hair-like strokes, and the technician plans the brow shape by measuring both sides and agreeing the design with the client.
